key_insight: Jev was fast, inexpensive, and well calibrated on some medical QA tasks, but its diagnostic performance dropped notably on harder exam-style and case-based benchmarks.
clinical_relevance: This suggests a constrained-answer AI may be useful for narrow medical QA support, but it needs task-specific validation before any clinical deployment.
method: Benchmarked Jev 1.13 on 4 medical datasets: MetaMedQA, PubMedQA, DiagnosisArena-MCQ, and NEJM Case Challenges.
Compared performance against GPT-6 Sol with and without medium reasoning.
Evaluated top-1 accuracy, calibration, selective prediction, and recognition of unanswerable questions.
evidence_signal: Across 8,469 requests, Jev matched GPT-6 Sol on PubMedQA, was better calibrated on MetaMedQA, but was substantially less accurate on DiagnosisArena-MCQ and NEJM cases.
watch_item: Because Jev can only choose from predefined answers, its output may be unreliable for nuanced or ambiguous clinical scenarios and should not be assumed clinically valid without local validation.
paper_title: Jev in Medicine: A Benchmark Evaluation. Preliminary Results
